articles.text: Editor: In May 2018 the Tennis Pickleball sub-committee was formed. They worked diligently over seven months. Their report was adopted by the Recreation Commission on January 16, 2019 and City Council on March 4, 2019. The critical recommendations ….were: (1) an open play system for pickleball, (2) City staff should work with PUSD to explore the creation of permanent pickleball courts at the Middle School sport courts. Subsequently the City paid $50,000 for court repaving. The wisdom of adopting open play is evident with the rapid growth of pickleball: a new vibrant community has been created. There have been no comments or complaints concerning the open play system until the start of the trial to dedicate the Linda tennis courts to pickleball. Now opponents of pickleball in Piedmont wish to negate important previous community work by imposing a reservation system. [The] attempt to remove the long-established open play system is an unneeded distraction from the real issues of what best serves our community. Pickleball opponents wish to eliminate out of town players by imposing a reservation system. Pickleball in Piedmont welcomes all demographics. As City Planner Kevin Jackson stated concerning the housing element: “I am proud to say that this community has embraced the State’s call to welcome more people of all backgrounds in Piedmont.” Piedmont pickleball has been doing that since 2018. As preeminent tennis writer Joel Drucker states: “Pickleball features something frequently missing from tennis: laughter.” Sores of residents now have new friends. Piedmont pickleball checks off all boxes of good public policy: a far more efficient use of limited racquet court space, significantly enhanced older adult programming, integrating neighborhoods and ages which builds community. Piedmont pickleball counters… bad press that Piedmont endures. Imposing a reservation system will significantly reduce player numbers and achieve the goal of Linda Beach opponents: we will not need the space. articles.text: I was up early on Sunday morning, September 11th. A busy day was ahead. The lead television news stories of the morning were of the motorcade carrying the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II through Scotland and somber observances in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania commemorating the 21st anniversary of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. Both stories served as reminders that grief and gratitude are frequent traveling companions. There was an outpouring of grief from people around the globe upon the death of the 96-year-old Queen of England. In Scotland, people lined the roadways as her coffin passed. With the grief there were also many expressions of gratitude for her fidelity to her work, her years as a global leader, her humor and her delight in her four-legged friends. As the motorcade carrying her coffin traversed the Scottish countryside, it was clear that grief and gratitude traveled together. At the sites of the September 11 attacks the dead were remembered, the first responders were honored, hymns were sung, prayers were offered, and speeches were made. All were fitting expressions of the profound grief of that day, the persistent grief that is with us still. Yet, with the grief, there was gratitude. There was gratitude for the courage, the compassion, the connecting which the tragedies evoked. There was gratitude for the rebuilding that has taken place. There was gratitude for the restoration that continues. The Piedmont Post remains available online to all subscribers, no matter where they live. In the Psalms, expressions of grief often give way to songs of gratitude. Psalm 74 is an excellent example. This communal prayer originated with the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of its temple in 586 BCE. articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division invites community members to celebrate Earth Day by offering free compost at the City’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue at Red Rock Road this Saturday, April 22. Residents may pick up one cubic yard of free compost per household between 9 a.m. and 12 p.m. while supplies last. Residents will need to bring a shovel, gloves, and container for their compost. Volunteers and Public Works staff will be on hand to help with bagging and loading. Optional pre-registration is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ CompostGiveaway. The compost originally came from yard trimmings and food waste that Piedmonters and other communities serviced by Republic Services put in their green waste bins. Republic Services takes this waste to a large-scale facility where it is transformed into compost. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. In addition to the Earth Day event, free self-haul compost is available to residents every Friday outside the Corporation Yard. For more information see piedmont.ca.gov/CompostProgram. For questions contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont. ca.gov. articles.text: – Dr. Mark Jacobson Guest lecturer, Climate Speaker Series On April 5th, the Piedmont League of Women Voters and Piedmont Connect presented the sixth and final event in their joint 2022-23 Climate Speaker Series. This month’s lecture and discussion was given by award-winning scientist, author and Stanford professor Dr. Mark Jacobson. He spoke on the technologies and actions needed to provide 100% of the world’s energy with clean, stable, renewable energy. sensus developed by the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (UN IPCC), a reduction of our emissions by 80% by 2030 and 100% by 2050 is needed to prevent a global average temperature rise of more than 1.5 degree Centigrade. Electric appliances – both heating/ cooling appliances as well as electric vehicles (EVs) – are much more energy efficient than their fossil-or-biofuel-burning equivalents. For example, electric heat pumps use 25% of the energy of natural gas furnaces or water heaters. Similarly, EVs are 4 times more efficient than internal-combustion engines. This is important given that 11.3% of all global energy use is expended to mine, refine, and transport fossil fuels and uranium. Jacobson also described the various available existing technologies to power heavy industry, provide long-haul transportation, and store power. Fuel cells can be used for air travel, shipping, long-haul trucking and military transports when battery EVs (BEVs) become less viable. There are several colors used to classify how hydrogen is developed into a fuel. Jacobsen demystified this hydrogen color spectr um, explaining that only green hydrogen is a positive and efficient solution to the climate crisis and that so-called “blue,” “pink,” “turquoise,” “gray,” “brown” or “black” hydrogen are not. Only green hydrogen, or hydrogen produced from clean, fossil-free, renewable energy sources, is a fuel compatible with retaining stable global climate conditions. In addition, the costs of global warming impacts – from wildfires, extreme heat and storms, ocean acidification, vector borne diseases, agricultural shifts and rising sea levels – are expected to rise each year, incurring another $30 trillion by 2050. As fossil fuels become less plentiful, more expensive and difficult to extract and process, price increases coupled with the concentrated control of the resource will lead to increasing levels of social and economic instability and geopolitical conflicts. He presented data that showed using fossil fuels for energy needs is costly, destabilizing, and ecologically ruinous. articles.text: In advance of its participation in the Big Climb event at Oracle Park in San Francisco on Friday, April 29, the Piedmont Fire Department is helping raise donations for the nonprofit Leukemia and Lymphoma Society. PFD is registered for the event in the First Responders category along with other law enforcement, emergency medical workers, and other firefighting teams. Piedmont’s 4-man team will climb approximately 2,000 steps in Oracle Stadium, from the bottom of right field to the top and end of left field, to raise awareness and critical funds for blood cancer research and patient support. As of April 17, the Piedmont firefighters had raised $625 of its goal of $2,000. Last year’s Big Climb teams raised an average of $600 each. Led by Fire Captain Justin McNulty, Piedmont’s team includes firefighters Nicholas Christ, Anthony Renteria, and Brian Protheroe, Since registering for the event last December, the team has been training continually. “We run the stairs at Witter Field and Blair, constantly running laps, laps, laps,” explained McNulty. “At the firehouse, we’ve been doing step training every shift, at least three to four times a week. We have a gym stair-stepping machine in our fitness center in the basement, and I put in about 25 minutes every night.” Although this is the first year that the PFD has participated in the Big Climb, he and others in the department have taken part in many similar fitness competitions over the course of his 21 years with the department. “We often do CrossFit challenges; three of us did one in Rocklin recently. We’re encouraged by the fact that much of the physical fitness equipment in our basement is already the kind used to train for these competitions,” he added. “It’s all about the camaraderie and teambuilding for us.” Often participating in the federally funded, internationally touring [annual] Firefighter Combat Challenge, McNulty himself won two world titles with the Northern California team in 2008 and 2009. “For the First Responder teams, the Leukemia Society made a plaque which will be awarded to the team with the fastest three members’ times put together. We’ve been training especially hard, wanting to earn the plaque.” “For me it’s also about promoting the importance of fitness for our firefighters,” McNulty added. “No matter how light the equipment gets, no matter how much the technology advances, physical fitness is still at the center of how well we can perform. The fact that everything we fundraise for this competition is going to such a good cause is a great motivator.” Describing the nonprofit’s efforts to change the face of blood cancer, Christ wrote on his fundraising webpage that “LLS’ continued advancements over the years are responsible for the blood cancer survival rate doubling and tripling; in some cases, the survival rate has even quadrupled. And many LLS supported therapies not only help blood cancer patients but are now used to treat patients with rare forms of stomach and skin cancers. They’re even being tested in clinical trials for patients with a range of cancers including lung, brain, breast, pancreatic and prostate cancers.” All donations are tax deductible, and may be made by clicking on bit.ly/3UIefdH.

articles.text: Renovation of the steps at the eastern edge of Piedmont Park by Highland Avenue and Guilford Road is expected to conclude by the first week of May. The project, which began on January 23, was originally expected to conclude in midMarch; however, rainstorms created delays of more than one month. The $155,000 renovation project was approved by City Council on September 6, 2021, with $55,000 of the cost being paid by Piedmont Beautification Foundation and Piedmont Garden Club. “The main priority of this project is safety,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “The contractor will replace the current steps – wooden railroad ties of varying sizes – with colored concrete steps and landings and add metal handrails on both sides of the steps and landings.” Further additions to the site include benches, trees, and a small plaza with a permeable-pavement floor to accommodate for groundwater runoff. The park entrance at the corner of Highland and Guilford is fenced off until work is completed. Details and a design of the steps is available online at bit.ly/ 3jlK65z. articles.text: Girls ages 2-18 from across the Bay Area are invited to participate in the 2nd annual Play Like a Girl event in Piedmont on Sunday, April 23, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Witter Field. This fun day of demonstrations and hands-on activities is free to all and offers opportunities to practice pitching, hitting, shooting hoops and even rowing with the guidance of skilled athletes and coaches. The main stage will feature live demonstrations at half-hour intervals. Attendees can try sports ranging from baseball to boxing to ultimate frisbee at 20 stations. The event also includes a Q&A session, photo ops, and meet-and-greet opportunities with professional women athletes and female Olympians, including 7-time Olympic medalist Dana Vollmer, professional soccer player Miranda Nild, professional volleyball player Mandy Bible, and former Olympic rower Liz Behrens of Piedmont. Last year’s event attracted over 400 participants. To register or to sign up as a volunteer, visit piedmont.ca.gov/playlikeagirl. Lifelong benefits Participation in sports builds skills that support girls throughout their lives, teaching leadership, discipline, and teamwork. Girls who participate in sports experience lower rates of depresThe second annual Play Like a Girl event will be on Sunday, April 23 sion and higher self-esteem than their non-athlete peers. • Girls who participate in sports are significantly more likely to graduate high school compared to non-athletes. The correlation is particularly strong for African American and Latinx girls. • Young girls who play sports have higher grades and score higher on standardized tests than non-athletes. • Girls who participate in high school sports earn higher wages than non-athlete peers. Play Like a Girl is a Recreation Department initiative to empower young women through athletics. The Department’s “Try (it) Out Tuesdays” event series gives girls of all skill levels the opportunities to try new sports, meet coaches, ask questions, and learn about opportunities within the community throughout the year. Piedmont Recreation’s Title IX basketball jersey initiative was recently recognized by the California Park & Recreation Society as “Outstanding JEDI Program or Event” of the year. Each jersey for the 450 youth participants in the Department’s citywide elementary and middle school basketball league was numbered after a woman who pushed the boundaries of what is possible in basketball, from early pioneers to outstanding players and coaches of today. When they received their jerseys, the students also got a printed card explaining the significance of their number and the player who wore it. articles.text: Piedmont’s School Board issued a resolution on April 4 declaring gun violence a public health crisis. The resolution states “gun violence is a public health crisis that adversely impacts our students, our teachers, our families, and our communities.” The resolution directs the Superintendent to disseminate material on an annual basis stressing the importance of secure storage of firearms. This material will be included in the registration packet at the student walk through and will require parent or guardian acknowledgment of receipt. articles.text: On an overcast and blustery weekend, Troop 11 recently headed to Dillon Beach for an overnight campout. Famous for its huge sand dunes, Dillon Beach on the Sonoma Coast has long been a favorite destination for Scouts for sand surfing and firing off small rockets. “Playing on the dunes was my favorite!” shared many Scouts, who had come prepared with saucer sleds. As always, the rockets were popular, with adult volunteers on hand to help show Scouts how to set up rockets for a safe launch. Scouts had the opportunity to choose from three categories of engine, from “A” with less power to “C” with considerably more. “A” and “B” engines had the advantage of not going as high – and making it less of a trek to retrieve the rocket. “C” engines had more power and sent the rockets higher into the sky. “They always pick a C engine!” commented Bart Myers. Sunmi Yoo and Cassidy Carter high five after successfully lighting a fire. Piedmont Troop 11 Scout dad Bart Myers shares insight with Mason Myers as he prepares to launch his rocket. Anna Benson (left) and Annabelle Malione practice their fire-building skills under the guidance of Scoutmaster Rob Kobal. Jim Crawford-Jakubiak talks Fred Leonard through the process of connecting his rocket to the launchpad. Seonho Lee chops up an onion for the Fred Patrol’s tacos. The Sour Bacon Patrol of Nick Steimle (left), Senan Brodie, Theo Ferguson, Zach Osborn, and Drew Kobal begins preparing their Golden Spatula meal. “It’s an acquired taste,” explained Drew Kobal in a measured tone. The weekend was the first campout for Scouts who joined Troop 11 during open house season earlier this year. In addition to participating in other activities, the newest Scouts had a chance to earn their Totin’ Chip and Firem’n Chit, which gives new Scouts a foundation in how to safely use knives and axes, and how to safely start and put out a campfire. After a windy night that kept many Scouts awake, they were happy to make breakfast and break camp – but not before a long-held Scout tradition of cleaning the beach before heading home. Colin Amen (left) and Eric Venner put the finishing touches on burying Theo Ferguson in the sand. After setting up camp, the Scouts prepared for the troop’s Golden Spatula competition. They were evaluated on budget, taste, presentation, nutrition, teamwork, and cleanliness. A trio of adult volunteers served as judges and provided feedback at the evening campfire. The Sour Bacon Patrol took top honors this time with a delicious dish of homemade mac ‘n cheese that included broccoli, bacon, and a breadcrumb topping. It was cooked in a Dutch oven and dished up for the enthusiastic Scouts. The dinner was accompanied by a dessert that defied category but included Jello and sprite. “It’s actually pretty good!” said Theo Ferguson. The evening mist caught the light as Troop 11 Scouts perform a skit during the campfire program. Drew Kobal sleds down a steep sand dune. Scouts clamber along the beachside dunes during a litter pickup before leaving Dillon Beach.

articles.text: Frequent readers of the Post’s PPD Blue may have noticed a trend in which cars set off the Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPR) when entering the city. Hyundais and Kias account for nearly half of all stolen cars entering the city and triggering an ALPR. The ALPR devices scan cars with stolen or lost license plates, cars wanted for crimes, and cars without license plates. This is not a Piedmont phenomenon, it is linked to security defects which cause Kia and Hyundais to be easily hotwired and stolen. Viral TikTok videos, made in May of 2022 have increased the trend, by showing just how easily one of these cars can be stolen. Some thieves can steal such a vehicle with only a screwdriver and a USB chord. Between March 10 and March 24, the Piedmont Police log identified 42 ALPR triggers. Thirty-three of the cars were identified by make, and of those, 17 were activated by Kia or Hyundai vehicles. In the same two-week period three of the six vehicles stolen from Piedmont were Kia or Hyundai. The statistics are not an anomaly; a disproportionate number of Kia and Hyundai vehicles are being stolen. A report from Berkeley in March 2023 showed 38% of all stolen cars in that city were Kias or Hyundais. Both auto manufacturing companies are in South Korea; Hyundai is the parent company of Kia. Many of their cars use the same parts and some models are almost identical, like the Hyundai Elantra and the Kia Forte. Kia and Hyundai vehicles made in 2010-2021 were built without engine immobilizers. The common electronic security devices is standard with most other cars made since 2010, and ensures that a car can be started only when the driver’s keyless fob is present. While the Piedmont Police Department does not track ALPR hits by car make, the police have seen more stolen cars entering the city, more stolen vehicle recoveries and more ALPR related arrests in general. Statistics of stolen vehicle recoveries, the value of the recovered vehicles and arrests related to License Plate Readers. “The number [of ALPR hits] is climbing each year,” confirmed Police Captain Chris Monahan. Two years ago in 2021 the police recovered 59 stolen vehicles, and made 30 arrests related to ALPR triggers. Last year, in 2022, the numbers increased to 69 recovered stolen vehicles and 48 ALPR related arrests. Two weeks ago on April 2, an attempted catalytic converter theft by suspects in a silver Kia sedan was interrupted by a Piedmont resident on Florada Avenue. The suspect pointed a Glock handgun at the resident before speeding off into Oakland. This event has prompted the police to urge residents to avoid altercations during crimes in progress. In explaining the current police protocol for pursuit of a stolen vehicle, Capt. Monahan said, “We will not pursue a car if ‘all it is’ is stolen.” said Monahan. “There needs to be a much higher-level crime to warrant a pursuit. The potential for danger during pursuit is high and car thieves can be highly unpredictable.” Owners of Kia or Hyundai can check with the dealership to see if a free fix can be performed as part of a software update rollout in response to the increase in thefts. The update lengthens the time the alarm goes off, from 30 seconds to one minute, and makes it necessary for the key to be in the ignition switch for the vehicle to start. Many Kia and Hyundai dealerships are overwhelmed with demand for this service. Other options include buying an aftermarket alarm or a battery disconnect item with a kill-switch, something that can be purchased for around $15. articles.text: Prior to spring break, Piedmont High’s baseball team split a pair of games with Western Alameda County Conference opponent Alameda. The Highlanders defeated the Hornets at Alameda 3-2 on Tuesday, April 4 but lost 7-3 two days later at home at Humphries Diamond. PHS coach Eric Olson called the loss to Alameda unusual and felt his players may have been looking to their weeklong Spring Break the following week. “We’re going to call this an aberration; I don’t think I’ve seen us play like that all season. We need to tighten things up, because it was the same thing against Berkeley where we win the first game and get beaten the second time,” said Olson. Piedmont returns from break with a game tonight, April 19, at Bishop O’Dowd. Two days later it returns home against the Dragons to close out the series. 3-2 over Alameda Piedmont scored once in the top of the first inning and one more in the top of the third, but Alameda tied the game at 2-2 in the bottom of the third. The game remained deadlocked until Piedmont scored the game-winning run in the top of the sixth. Michael Aikawa pitched a complete game with four strikeouts and no earned runs. With one out in the first inning, sophomore Markos Lagios smacked a triple on the second pitch of his at bat to the left field fence. After Peter Krumins drew a walk, Will Parker Staff Photos Ryan McConathy smacked a onerun home run against Alameda. hit a single to left field to bring in Lagios. However, Piedmont ended the inning stranding Krumins at third. In the top of the third, Lagios led off with a double. With two outs, Lagios made his way to third on a mishandled pitch by the catcher, who subsequently threw the ball into the outfield when trying to throw Lagios out at third—allowing him to come home. With the game tied 2-2 going into the top of the sixth, Krumins led off with a single to right field while Parker reached first after smacking a hard ground ball to the second baseman, forcing an error. Krumins then scored in a fielder’s choice after Dimitri Papahadajopolous hit a ground ball to second. Aikawa put them down 1-2-3 in the bottom-of-the-sixth, but the bottom of the seventh was tense. articles.text: Playing in Vallejo on Monday, April 17, Piedmont was overwhelmed by St. Patrick on its first day back from Spring Break, 20-10. The high-scoring game looked more like a football result than softball. It marked the team’s seventh consecutive loss. In what generously is described as a rebuilding season, the team is trying to fill the vacancies of last year’s starting pitcher, Izzy Epstein, catcher Chiarra Lundin, Ginger Gardner and backup pitcher Annabelle Castronovo. Without pitchers, coach Gene Dennard has been forced to use players with no previous experience on the mound. Miya Fujimoto, for example, is this year’s starting pitcher after being the starting shortstop last year as a freshman. She was the Post’s 2022 Freshman of the Year for her contributions at shortstop, a position typically reserved for the team’s best glove. “When Miya is on the mound, it takes away one of our best infielders. She was our starting shortstop last year, we’d much rather have her in the field,” confirmed Dennard. Piedmont’s record now dips to 2-7-1 after making the jump to the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division, where they are 0-5 versus league teams. articles.text: Piedmont senior Parker Long has announced he intends to continue his track career in the fall at California Polytechnic State University in San Luis Obispo. Long’s winning time of 1:53.25 in the 800-meter run at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18 was enough to catch the attention of coaches at the Division 1 school. “It’s a good school academically; I think that’s what made me want to go there more than the other schools I was considering,” Long said. “This is a school that has a really good running program and educational system. I really didn’t think I would get in, honestly. I reached out after [the run at] Dublin. They said they were really impressed and wanted me on the team,” said Long. Long is currently No. 3 among Piedmont High’s all-time 800- meter runners. He is narrowly behind The Post’s 2018 Athlete of the Year, Reece Proctor, and Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer, Gordon Johnson. Top-five 800-meter runners: 1. Gordon Johnson, 1:51.10 (1989) 2. Reece Proctor, 1:52.64 (2018) 3. Parker Long, 1:53.25 (2023) 4. Cooper Downing, 1:53.40 (2022) 5. John Weber, 1:55.26 (2010) Long considered attending the University of Oregon as a student, but now found a school where he can competed while also enjoying his college experience at a deeper level than some other candidates. “I was considering a lot of the UC’s and my main one for a while was Oregon, not necessarily as a runner, but just because I liked the campus. Once I got into contact with Cal Poly, they made it sound really good. Then I went to check out the school and it really checked all of the boxes. It’s a little bit warmer {than Eugene] and it’s a unique city,” said Long. Parker plans on majoring in math, but knows he has time to figure out his academic future. Parker and the Piedmont High track team still have a lot of running left. The Western Alameda County Conference championship is on May 5, followed by the North Coast Section Bayshore Finals on May 13, NCS Meet of Champions on May 19-20, and CIF State Championship on May 26-27. Heading into the latter stage of the season, Long is hopeful to hit his peak at the right time and Parker Long, Class of 2023, is set to continue his running career with Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo. avoid fizzling out ahead of the state meet in Fresno. “The big sequence is league championships to the NCS region meet, then to NCS Finals, then to State. As we get closer to those races, I have to think about when I peak with my training. What happens with a lot of runners is they are super ambitious and over-train too early, and they end up dying out before the end of the season. Sometimes runners peak too late as well. I’m trying to find the sweet spot of those two things and peak exactly at the right time,” said Long. Parker Long is currently Piedmont High School’s third fastest all-time 800-meter runner with a time of 1:53.25. pages.text: Wednesday, Aprl 19, 2023 15 HIKING WITH JON Sibley Regional’s springtime splendor By Jonathan Comeaux It’s springtime in the Bay Area and blooms of wildflowers abound throughout the entire state. It makes the sun-swept hills of Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve in the Oakland Hills the perfect place to take in the scenery of the colorful plants and flowers. Sibley is most known for its stone labyrinths, but sunny days following the recent rain has allowed vegetation to grow and keep the hills green. Throughout Sibley Regional, the sharp contrasting orange of California Poppies and purple of Silver Lupine bushes sweep through the hills. Cows have been allowed to graze throughout the park in recent months, resulting in fewer poppies than previous years, but there are still many thickets of orange flowers. Sibley’s Round Top Loop trail is about 2.5 miles and connects to the Quarry and Volcanic trails, where you can find the labyrinths Photos by Jonathan Comeaux A California Poppy nestled in between Silver Lupine at Sibley Regional Volcanic Preserve The Mazzariello Labyrinth is the most famous attraction at Sibley Regional Preserve, which was created in 1989. Another labyrinth with more purple Silver Lupine bushes and poppies springing up on the The rolling hills towards Round Top, an extinct volcano that provides the volcanic rock throughout the park hillside and other geological features. The park is a popular area for dog walkers and is child friendly. After the loop trail connects to the Volcanic Trail, veer to the right to find the first quarry pit. It will be trail marker No. 2 on the park information pamphlet’s selfguided tour. Old quar r y operations removed massive basalt lava and exposed the interior of the Round Top volcano. The base of the pit consists of bedded tuff-breccias, which is volcanic ash and sedimentary rock fragments. The labyrinth featured at the base of the pit was originally created by Montclair sculptor Helena Mazzariello in 1989. It is the largest of the four stone mazes and is the most photographed spot in the entire park. Continuing on the Quarry Trail just 0.2 from the Mazzariello Labyrinth overlook is another labyrinth. Trail marker No. 5 on the tour is the second-largest labyrinth off of Volcanic Trail. When you reach a fork in the road with the Quarry Trail on the left, head to the right and take a slight uphill walk towards the pit. This one has a smaller heart shaped labyrinth but also a nearly vertical chunk of lava sticking out of the north end of the quarry. This pit was also created by the removal of massive basalt lava. In addition to dog walking, it is a great place to spark your child’s interest in geology. It also won’t be too taxing on their legs given the trail contains minor uphill portions. There is a large parking lot with free parking and a visitor’s center that displays various types of volcanic rocks and clean restrooms. Park at Huckleberry Botanical Sibley Regional is among the most popular parks in the Oakland Hills, often resulting in a crowded parking lot cars parked on Skyline Boulevard. If you’re willing to add 1.8 miles to the day with 600 feet in elevation gain, park at Huckleberry Botanical Regional Preserve. Hiking along the Huckleberry Loop trail until it merges with the Skyline Trail takes visitors to Sibley’s Round Top Loop trail. Taking a right turn adds another .18 of a mile to the hike and adds another 100 feet in elevation gain. Hugging Skyline Boulevard on our custom loop back to the car from Huckleberry to each of the hill-peaks at Sibley creates a 4.79-mile loop with 1,033 feet in elevation gain, and can be done in slightly less than two hours. Here is the map of The Posts’ 4.79 mile loop from Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve to Sibley Regional and back. Starting your day at Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve adds some shade to your hike and is a bit more hidden than Sibley. Follow the signs toward Sibley Regional from Huckleberry. articles.text: SF Jazz will host its annual gala on Thursday, May 3, when it celebrates SF Jazz Founder and Executive Artistic Director Randall Kline. The gala will feature performances by Ambrose Akinmusire, Regina Carter, Rosanne Cash and John Leventhal, Ravi Coltrane, Herbie Hancock, Eric Harland, Branford Marsalis, Cécile McLorin Salvant and Sullivan Fortner. Dianne Reeves will serve as host, with after-party performances by Trombone Shorty and Red Baraat. There will be a live free broadcast of the after-party concert at 8:30 p.m. on May 4. articles.text: The self-driving orchestra, with vacant podium, has arrived at center stage. Credit composer Brian Baumbusch, 35, from Alameda – along with a Covid quarantine, electronics and a touch of Indonesia. Yes, finally, one tiny benefit we gained from that scourge of a Covid virus, leads to some invention and dispersion of musical ideas. Marooned in a Djakarta quarantine last year, Baumbusch composed his Polytempo Music which was premiered in San Francisco on April 13 by the elite S.F. Contemporary Music Players. His inspiration relegated conductor Eric Dudley to a front-row seat looking on while the dozen musicians played their parts guided by electronic click tracks in earphones, set to such a variety of energetic beats and tempos as to be impossible to conduct. It may sound like total chaos. But no, Baumbusch took his lead from Indonesian gamelan music, where slow and fast tempos are overlaid (a bit like Bach’s “Sleepers Awake” or “Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring”), and maintained some harmonic control. This adroit derringdo led to an engrossing world premiere at the Taube Atrium, full of dense overlay and ear-caressing music. The work was fast paced, with striking harmonic shifts, all a coherent dazzle of sound we need to hear again, then ending on a dime. The impetus for revivals remains there, as the 18 minutes The concert opened with a live-instrument arrangement of the late expat Conlon Nancarrow’s Study No. 3a for sextet, with clarinetist Jeff Anderle at the forefront. The arrangement counters Nancarrow’s original musical thrust and method, wherein he had been totally mechanical – all inscribed on hand-cut player-piano rolls, usually intent on defying human capabilities of play. A rare aspect of the stellar conductor Esa-Pekka Salonen was on view with his septet, Catch and Release (2006). Focusing on this 25-minute work was challenged by the distracting, near-bare-chested attire on one player. Please, less distraction and tedium, more decorum! Salonen’s audacity led him to use an unsettling, unorthodox ensemble, whose trumpet, trombone and drumming overwhelmed the strings and woodwinds. Nimble percussionist Haruka Fujii had to fast-step between the drums and a more ingratiating vibraphone. Its finale offered an exercise in staccato, ever more intense. Artistic director Dudley is an amiable conductor with a nonstop smile, frequently bending his knees, seemingly irresistibly impelled by rhythms. NOTES S.F. Contemporary Music Players in its 52nd season with Baumbusch premiere, Nancarrow and Salonen, at the Taube Atrium Theater, San Francisco April 13. Online: info@sfcmp.org. Composer Brian Baumbusch presented here comprised only about one-third of the entire opus, according to one participant. Dudley got up to lead a codicil section with an evolved waltz looming in the mist wafting over – a calm after a windstorm, akin to the storm-scene effect in Beethoven’s Sixth Symphony. Tranquility restored. The evolution of “Polytempo Music” was not the sole fruit of the quarantine. Covid actually encouraged the isolation of the musicians, who learned their parts separately at home, then assembled less for rehearsals and more for sound checks and click audibility. Again, Covid forced musical innovation. During the performance the guidance came from an upstage laptop, with the composer herding all the electronics like sheep. Unplug the laptop and the premiere would be lost – we live and die by PG&E. Some prerecorded tracks also filtered in via loudspeakers overhead. The Cancer League, Inc. thecancerleague

articles.text: Summer vacation is rapidly arriving. Have you made summer plans for your musical kids? Music camps are taking reservations, and some deadlines have already passed. This article is a reminder to make your reservations. Tempus fugit, as the Romans used to say. Music camps in U.S. One of the greatest experiences I ever had was at the Idyllwild Music Camp when I was in the eighth grade. Idyllwild, which is high above Palm Spring, seems to have fallen by the wayside, but there are other camps that will be of interest. Interlochen Music Camp in Michigan is probably the biggest and the most famous in the United States. It offers sessions in all art categories and has a huge enrollment of international scope. Berklee School of Music is another enterprise of international scope. They have campuses in the eastern United States and also in Europe. The Aspen Music Festival in Colorado has operated since 1949 and has a very good reputation. There are also two fine music camps in our area. Cazadero is the more famous. It is located at Russian River, and for many years has maintained its high standards. Everyone I know has spoken well of the experience. La Honda Music Camp is about an hour away from Piedmont in the Santa Cruz Mountains. I was an instructor there some years ago. It was lots of fun for me, and the kids had a good time. Activities include ensembles both large and small, with intensive instrumental instruction. Jazz is a featured element in addition to classical music. The food is good and there are lots of activities. International music camps Two international music camps come to mind. The fine violinist Emil Altschuler has a summer music camp, Altschuler Summer Music Institute, in Rimini, a resort city in Italy. Emil has patterned his music camp around the ideals of Jascha Heifetz. ASMI emphasizes string instruments. Cristiana Pegoraro, who is well known to Piedmont audiences, continues her excellent Narnia Music Festival in Narnia, Italy. To me, the Narnia program encompasses just about everything that I look for. In the first place, it is an all-encompassing music festival. There is a Festival Orchestra and concerts of all kinds. Some of the concerts feature notable concert performers and the students get many opportunities to perform. While music is featured, everyone has the opportunity to study foreign languages, learn about the local history and go on tours. This barely scratches the surface. Narnia is located about an hour north of Rome. It is a beautiful area and also a famous culinary center. Please take my advice: Make your plans and do it soon. Meanwhile back home at the PCA Fine concerts continue apace in our Piedmont Center for the Arts. Last Saturday, the Diluvian Quartet played. They might even be considered the “in House Quartet“ in the Center since they play there so often. The program was rather brief; Mozart’s famous Quartet in D Minor opened the program and Gliere’s String Quartet No. 2 closed the program. Even though my son is a member of the quartet, I feel that I can be objective in my opinions. Diluvian plays with great discipline and attention to musical balance. It is obvious that they enjoy making music. At the conclusion of the concert, the large and faithful audience burst into vociferous applause. That spoke volumes. articles.text: Kiersey Clemons and Nick Offerman star in Hearts Beat Loud Movies too often barely dip below the surface, satisfied with a superficial patina of affluence or Disneyesque fantasy, the writing resulting in a coarsening failure of language and imagination. Others are replete with pulp cinema action (read violence and a high body count) that can seem a betrayal of film as a possible art form. But there are those small gems that quietly slip into theaters and, remarkably, find that sweet spot while exploring the human condition, such as it is, in a way that resonates. Hearts Beat Loud is exactly such a film, tenderly told, a narrative that focuses on a father-daughter relationship that feels honest and perfectly imperfect. Frank Offerman portrays Frank Fisher, a crusty, single parent, middle-aged, who has had a record store in Red Hook Brooklyn for 17 years. His daughter, Sam (Kiersey Clemmons), is about to leave for UCLA in California with the goal of becoming a doctor. Frank is already feeling like an empty nester, a certain loneliness closing in as he prepares to shut the doors of his record shop for good. But suddenly change is inserting itself into his life – the life of a once rocker, now a dad to a gifted, precocious teen who can act more adult-like than Frank. Sam is also exploring a new relationship with a young artist and gallerista, Rose (Sasha Lane), who is deeply connected to New York. Since she was 12, they have spent evenings jamming. During one such session they create a single record, Hearts Beat Loud, that unexpectedly takes off on Spotify. It proves to be an intoxicating collaboration, a song filled with emotion, with lyrics and music written and sung by Sam, whose lovely voice soars. Frank is captivated and those long ignored feelings that he missed the train some two decades back return and a nudging hope returns: perhaps he will have a second chance. He gives their 2-person music combo the name We’re Not a Band. What is so moving about this film is that every moment that Sam and Frank have together on screen feels true. Authentic. It’s no small thing. Relationships between parents and teens can be both dynamic and a puzzle within a puzzle, In a sense, the music listened to and created by Frank and Sam becomes part of the story’s dialogue and is a metaphor that repeatedly defines their connection. There is also another layer to Hearts Beat Loud, and that is the friendship Frank has with Dave (Ted Danson), a Brooklyn bar owner. Leaning forward, elbows resting on that long plank of oak, Dave behind the bar, Frank on a stool, they talk about the world. And it’s Dave who looks at Frank for a long moment and says, “When life hands you conundrums, you turn them into art.” That small morsel of wisdom reaches Frank who feels a bit buffeted by life and suddenly at loose ends. It’s a nice moment. As are those moments he spends with Leslie (Toni Collette), his landlord, who reaches out to him and realizes, after an unfortunate encounter, that his rough edges might need a bit of sanding. Hearts Beat Loud is a stirring affirmation, and the music is surprising and uplifting. Hearts Beat Loud. Directed by Brett Haley. Starring Nick Offerman, Kiersey Clemons, Ted Danson. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Spotlight is not a lament for that moment in journalistic history when ink on paper reporting was still the tip of the spear and valued above all else as a way to inform the public about community life and its institutions. There is nothing about this film that is mournful or melodramatic, which, given its subject matter, it could have been. Rather, it is a celebration of the role fine journalism has played in the health of our democracy, in this case the Boston Globe newspaper. Spotlight is also a newspaper procedural in which a shocking and wrenching story is first investigated and then, finally, going to press after some eight months of “shoe leather” research and interviews and tenacious digging and then waiting until all the pieces fit and the paper concludes unequivocally it had it right. Note that the recent film Truth was a story about the CBS investigation into George W. Bush’s military record. But it was rushed and ultimately the center could not hold and finally unraveled, ending careers. What the Globe did right was demonstrate a careful and granular deliberateness that eventually resulted in the journalists and the paper receiving a Pulitzer Prize. To its credit, the film avoids righteous indignation, histrionics, and all tantalizing speechifying. Rather it almost stoically conveys a tension defined by reluctance and anxiety and restraint as the reporters pursue a story that no one really wants to tell, yet for all those involved know must be told. It’s the very essence of the craft of journalism and defines the moral center of what it means to be a newspaper and newspaper reporter. The year is 2002. In the first set piece of the film, an editor is retiring from The Boston Globe, and staff and editors are waiting for the newly hired Editor-in-Chief, Marty Baron (Liev Shreiber), to arrive from the Miami Herald. One of the first stories that Baron wants the investigative team to revisit is an incident between a child and a local Catholic priest. The reporting team – Spotlight) – consists of Walter “Robbie” Robinson (Michael Keaton), Sacha Pfieffer (Rachel McAdams), Michael Rezendes (Mark Ruffalo) and Matt Carrol (Brian d’Arcy). With some initial reluctance, the team, led by Robinson, begins to peel, ever so painstakingly, an onion that unexpectedly becomes a massive story. It is an archival dig, involving interviews and clippings and city hall records. It means going to court, asking for the release of documents, and, above all, it means overcoming the community’s hostility and the Church’s stonewalling silence. Slowly, however, the team begins to realize that the initial event – one priest, one child – was not a one-off but represented the tip of an iceberg of behavior that reached from the Bishop’s office to the farthest corners of the archdiocese. In the aggregate, the story proves to be a seismic scandal involving the sexual abuse of countless children of Boston by priests. Gradually the reporters come to understand that it occurred because of the collusive response by the Catholic Church as priest after priest was moved from parish to parish, some placed on sick leave, others listed as simply on leave, while the Church used its power and influence to expunge the records and wrap itself in a cloak of conspiratorial secrecy. Spotlight is an astonishingly well-made film, and an example of what fine ensemble acting can achieve. There is no one actor who carries the film. There is only a solid group of actors, each creating a portrayal that is idiosyncratic, flawed and very human. As well, the film has a washedout feel to it, one created by claustrophobic newsrooms with dropped ceilings and fluorescent lighting as the camera holds consistent wide shots, rarely singling out any one individual. It might be hard to imagine that a procedural film, set in basements and stark rooms, could generate atmospherics akin to a murder mystery. And yet, that is exactly what Spotlight achieves. It’s a remarkable film. Spotlight. Directed by Tom McCarthy. Starring Mark Ruffalo, Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdam. 2 hrs., 7 min. Rated R. Released 2015. Now streaming on VUUDU/Prime/HBO MAX,

articles.text: A scene from Happy Feet Happy Feet is charming and playful, making this rollicking tale of a unique penguin named Mumble (Elijah Wood) seem decidedly fresh. Apparently, every Emperor penguin sings a unique song called a “heartsong,” used to attract a mate. If the males’ song matches the females’ song, well, they mate, which is what occurred with Mumble’s parents, Norma Jean (Nicole Kidman) and Memphis (Hugh Jackman). As a result, Norma Jean lays an egg, which she leaves in the care of Memphis while she and the other females go off to fish. It’s a harsh winter, and Memphis accidentally drops the egg. When the new chick, Mumble, is finally born, the parents discover that he can’t sing, but can tap dance. Mumble soon becomes a young adult whose feet never stop moving. The elders, led by Noah (Hugo Weaving), grumpily take exception to Mumble’s dancing and ridicule him for being different. Meanwhile, we learn that he has a secret crush on the talented Gloria (Brittany Murphy), but doesn’t have the “heartsong” that is so necessary to find a companion. Meanwhile, Mumble meets a group of mini-Mexican Adelie penguins, called “the Amigos,” whose leader is Ramon Lovelace (Robin Williams) who is willing to help Mumble court Gloria (Ramon sings “My Way” while Mumble lip-synchs). Naturally, Gloria falls for him. Soon all the young penguins are singing and tap dancing to “Boogie Wonderland.” The elders, of course, are appalled. Mumble is ordered to stop, but refuses, and is exiled from the flock, blamed for what has been a lean fishing season. And so Mumble’s adventure begins. It takes him all the way to Australia where he ends up in a marine sanctuary where kids, one girl in particular, can stand and watch him swimming behind massive glass panes. The girl taps on the glass and Mumble, with his beak, taps back, hoping to communicate with the humans. Event ually, Mumble is released from the sanctuary and finds his way home to his flock. Upon his return he challenges the elders and prevails, and soon everyone is dancing and celebrating, most especially Mumble and Gloria and Ramon. Happy Feet. Directed by George Miller. Voices of Elijah Wood, Robin Williams, Brittany Murphy. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG. Released in 2006. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/HBO MAX/ Apple tv.

articles.text: On ancient maps, when cartographers came to a part of the world that had yet to be explored, they would write, “Here Be Dragons.” What they could have written is “Here Be Beasts.” And it’s around such unknown places a mythology grew of intrepid seafarers who hunted these beasts, which is the sweet spot of Netflix’s brilliantly animated, photo-realistic The Sea Beast, nominated for an Oscar this year. At the center of this imaginative tale is an adventure-seeking, fierce, and delightful protagonist, 11-year-old Maisie Brumble (Zaris-Angel Hator) who runs away from an orphanage, determined to stow away on a magnificent square-rigger, one that is known to place itself in harm’s way as it searches the seas for monsters/ One monster in particular is known as the Red Buster. Maisie sneaks on board a ship with enormous red sails and helmed by the notorious one-eyed captain Crow (Jared Harris) who lost his eye in a battle with Red, Jacob Holland (voiced by Karl Urban) and Maisie Brumble (voiced by Zaris-Angel Hator) in The Sea Beast the fearsome dragon-like monster. Think of him as Ahab and Red Buster as the white whale. His first mate is Sarah Sharpe (Marianne Jean Baptiste). Of course, Maisie is soon discovered on board by the heroic Jacob Holland (Karl Urban), the future heir to captain Crow. And so the two set out on an exciting journey, finding an unexpected kinship, We soon learn that Jacob is also an orphan. The two are shipwrecked on a tropical island, they encounter a rival ship, the Imperator, captained by admiral Hornagold (Don Stevens), and encounter a bevy of perilous situations with a myriad of sea creatures. The Sea Beast is a rousing good yarn, set in the early 1700s, with remarkable visuals – constantly roiling seas, tentacled monsters that take umbrage at the intrusion of the likes of Crow or Hornagold. Kids will love this enthralling story, and they will take delight in the chutzapah of the adorable and vibrant Maisie. The Sea Beast. Animated. Directed by Chris Williams. With voices of Karl Urban, Zaris-Angel Hator, and Jared Harris. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated PG. Released 2022. Now streaming on Netflix

The Northern Rhone is considered the part of the river that stretches from Vienne south to just before Valence – some 40 miles. Last week I wrote about the northern part of the region focusing on the AVA’s of Cote Rotie and Condrieu home to some of the greatest Syrahs and Viogniers in the world. As we shift to the southern part of the region, Syrah remains the only red grape that is allowed, while the white wines shift from Viognier to Marsanne and RousThe M. Chapoutier tasting room in Tain l’Hermitage. The chapel on top of Hermitage hill sanne. These two powerhouse white grapes are used separately or sometimes blended to create intense long-lived succulent wines. Hermitage One of France’s most famous vineyard sites is Hermitage hill on the east bank of the Rhone across from the town of Tain. The river turns here and the hill, a granitic outcrop, and an extension of the Massif Central, faces south giving perfect exposure to ripen the grapes. Standing on the top of the hill next to the old stone chapel once home to a hermit, you sense that you are in a spiritual place – the spiritual home of the Syrah grape. It is believed that winemaking here goes back to the Roman times but there are no clear records before the 17th century. Hermitage was an official wine in the French courts of King Louis XIII and Louis XIV, and Thomas Jefferson stopped for a visit on his wine tour of France and praised the white wines made here. He even had some shipped back to his home in Virginia. M. Chapoutier A book I was handed simply said “M. Chapoutier Universe.” It is a catalogue of all the wines produced by Michel Chapoutier and his partners around the world. In addition to his massive work in the Rhone Valley, he has partnerships in Australia, Spain, Portugal, Germany and many non-Rhone parts of France, with hundreds and hundreds of wines. I have often heard Michel Chapoutier described as “energetic” but it’s hard to imagine how he can keep track of all of his ventures. Entering the stylish tasting room on a small street in Tain is like entering a temple devoted to wine. We were treated to a private tasting hosted by Michel’s son Maxime (who has developed his own line of beer called One Shot). The tasting began with a 15 euro Viognier that was refreshing and light. Ten wines later it ended with the Le Pavillion Ermitage, a 436 euro ($478) masterpiece of Syrah. After the tasting Maxine took us for lunch at the Ferraton winery overlooking the river. Ferraton is owned by Chapoutier but is managed separately and the house has its own style. After a lunch of grilled sardines, we had the opportunity to taste the Ferraton range of wines. I had never tasted their wines and was pleasantly surprised to discover they were an outstanding lineup. I was also glad to find out they are widely available in the US thanks to K&L Wines in San Francisco. See Wine Corner on page 30 Maxime Chapoutier conducts our tasting. The quaint village of Cornas. articles.text: Community members are invited to join the Walking on Wednesdays group on April 26 for a special docent-led tour of historic Mountain View Cemetery. The tour will be led by long-time Mountain View docent Dennis Evanosky, who has written two books about Oakland’s history, Oakland’s Mountain View Cemetery, and Oakland’s Laurel District. He has also written books about Alameda and San Francisco. The tour of the cemetery will include details of its section devoted to veterans of the Civil War. Besides its flowers and historic monuments, the cemetery has expansive views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco, which the walkers always also enjoy. Participants should plan to meet in front of Mountain View’s main mausoleum on Wednesday, April 26 at 10:30 a.m. The cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue at the end of Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. There is parking inside the cemetery. The tour will last for about 1 hour and 45 minutes. For more information, please contact Dick Carter at camktgrp@comcast.net. articles.text: The Piedmont Adult School is hosting a three-day Expo this weekend, Friday-Sunday, April 21-23 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia. The Adult School has dozens of affordable class options during its spring session, portions and aspects of the course offerings which will be on display during the Expo for the first time. A reception on Friday, April 21, from 5:00-8:00 p.m. will feature live demonstrations, complimentary food and an art exhibit of student work. It will provide an opportunity for the community to meet the instructors and learn more about the wide variety of classes offered by the Adult School. On Saturday and Sunday, April 22-23, from 11:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m., there will be open gallery hours to view the art exhibit. The expo is free and open to all. The open gallery runs concurrently with the Piedmont FoodFest on Sunday, which will be right around the corner at Piedmont Park. “The PCA is delighted to be working with the Adult School. We see this as a very logical collaboration to display the wide range of classes and activities they have. We hope this is beginning of a very wonderful relationship,” said Center for the Arts president Sue Malick. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a treat last week when architect Jim Kellogg led the group in the absence of Dick Carter. His topic was the introduction of Berkeley Arts and Crafts architecture to Piedmont between 1910 and 1926. He explained that Berkeley Arts and Crafts started with teaching, mentoring, and development of the Arts and Crafts movement by Bernard Maybeck in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He collaborated with and mentored three leading architects on whom the walk focused: John Galen Howard, Julia Morgan, and John Hudson Thomas. Morgan and Thomas met in the office of Howard. Morgan and Thomas became well recognized by the Berkeley School of Architecture. They adopted and built their practices around the Arts and Crafts movement, and each designed numerous notable single-family homes in Piedmont. Although Howard did not design any projects in Piedmont, his influence on Morgan and Thomas was important. Another architect Kellogg included in the tour was Albert Farr. He played a key role in master planning and building Piedmont during this period. His works included: the Piedmont Community Center, City Hall, the Christian Science Church (now The Piedmont Center for the Arts), the Exedra, Piedmont Community Church, and many single-family homes. All three of the famous architects practiced at the same time and designed projects in Piedmont. They had their own styles, and also client bases and political connections that influenced their careers. Morgan embraced arts and crafts and integrated it with classical design popular at that time. She was the first woman to receive a degree from the Beaux Arts School of Architecture in Paris, and the first women to become a registered architect in California. She became famous because of her employment by William Randolph Hearst to design Heart Castle. Thomas also embraced the arts and crafts movement and developed his own “exuberant style” of design and craftsman detailing. His career was focused on luxury single-family homes in the East Bay and San Francisco, but he did not have connections with people such as Hearst. Farr is well respected for his talent, but his style would be described as “eclectic.” The Piedmont Community Church masterpiece is pure California Mission style, but Farr also produced English Tudor, French Classical, as well as Arts and Crafts buildings depending on what his clients wanted. He lived in Piedmont for a while and became well connected with City government including Frank C. Havens which led to many important commissions. A large group of 37 walkers and three K-9 best friends participated in Walking on Wednesdays’ walk on March 12. articles.text: Lillian Rubenstein, a woman of style and grace, died at the age of 100 years and 8 months on April 4, 2023 in her home with her three children by her side. She passed away peacefully following a brief period of declining health with a large, smiling picture of her late husband Bob immediately next to her. Lillian was born on July 15, 1922 in Philadelphia. She was the only child of Ukrainian immigrants, Abe and Anna Cohen and was raised as an only child by her mother after her father passed away when she was only three months old. In the late 1920’s, Anna and Lillian came to California at the beginning of the Great Depression, ultimately finding their way to Stockton where Lillian was raised and schooled. She graduated from Stockton High at age 16. In the defining moment of her life, Lillian went to a youth gathering in Petaluma in May 1939 where by chance she met a shy, blond haired, blue-eyed 18-yearold boy from Oakland, Bob Rubenstein. She was as immediately and powerfully attracted to Bob as he was to her. They began a 2 1/2-year long-distance courtship between Stockton and Oakland that culminated on December 14, 1941, when the young couple was married. That day was the beginning of an idyllic, extraordinary almost fairytale relationship that ended only in 2018 when, after 76 1/2 years of a perfect, loving marriage, Bob passed away. Those many years were filled with as much joy, pleasure, happiness, fulfillment and love as any two people could possibly have enjoyed. During that time, the couple had three children, built a home in Piedmont in 1950 that they occupied until Lillian’s passing. They were fortunate enough to enjoy good health and life treated them very well. During their many years together, they created a large and loving family, formed countless extraordinarily close and enduring friendships and enjoyed many, many exciting, varied and wonderful life experiences together. Bob and Lillian complemented each other perfectly with Lillian’s active, outgoing, energetic and strong-willed personality contrasting perfectly and, as recently as last month, took a keen interest in the trials and tribulations of the Warriors. She was known for both her skill and competitiveness as a tennis player. Well into her 100th year, she remained an accomplished mahjong player who thoroughly enjoyed the company of the ladies with whom she played. Lillian and Bob were members of Temple Sinai continuously since 1956 and Claremont Country Club for over 25 years. In her younger years, she was an active member of her socially conscious sorority, Theta Delta Xi. In later years she devoted substantial time and energy to The Cancer League and Hoe and Hope community garden club. Lillian enjoyed the happiest and most fulfilling life one could ever hope to lead. She overcame the adversity of a difficult childhood and devoted her life to being the best, most dedicated and loving wife, mother and friend that she could possibly be. She lived a full and wonderful life. Lillian is predeceased by her ever-adoring husband Bob who passed away in 2018. She is survived by her three loving children, Ron (Erica), Craig (Terri) and Barbee, and by nine grandchildren, Jeff Rubenstein (Amie), Tracy Weis (Brett), Greg Rubenstein (Whitney), Lisa Sommer (Justin), Kim Radtke, Brian Rubenstein (Haleh), Morgan Nelson (Charlie), Mallory Johnston (John) and Tim Johnston (Courtney). She also leaves behind 15 precious great-grandchildren. The family particularly acknowledges and thank Dr. Dean Nickles for his extraordinary and attentive care, and caregivers Dhel Sanchez and Bambi Lao for the warm and compassionate care they gave Lillian during her final days. The family will be forever grateful. The family will host a gathering celebrating Lillian’s welllived 100 plus years on April 25. She passed away peacefully following a brief period of declining health with a large, smiling picture of her late husband Bob immediately next to her. Lillian was born on July 15, 1922 in Philadelphia. She was the only child of Ukrainian immigrants, Abe and Anna Cohen and was raised as an only child by her mother after her father passed away when she was only three months old. In the late 1920’s, Anna and Lillian came to California at the beginning of the Great Depression, ultimately finding their way to Stockton where Lillian was raised and schooled. She graduated from Stockton High at age 16. In the defining moment of her life, Lillian went to a youth gathering in Petaluma in May 1939 where by chance she met a shy, blond haired, blue-eyed 18-yearold boy from Oakland, Bob Rubenstein. She was as immediately and powerfully attracted to Bob as he was to her. They began a 2 1/2-year long-distance courtship between Stockton and Oakland that culminated on December 14, 1941, when the young couple was married. That day was the beginning of an idyllic, extraordinary almost fairytale relationship that ended only in 2018 when, after 76 1/2 years of a perfect, loving marriage, Bob passed away. Those many years were filled with as much joy, pleasure, happiness, fulfillment and love as any two people could possibly have enjoyed. During that time, the couple had three children, built a home in Piedmont in 1950 that they occupied until Lillian’s passing. They were fortunate enough to enjoy good health and life treated them very well. During their many years together, they created a large and loving family, formed countless extraordinarily close and enduring friendships and enjoyed many, many exciting, varied and wonderful life experiences together. Bob and Lillian complemented each other perfectly with Lillian’s active, outgoing, energetic and strong-willed personality contrasting perfectly and, as recently as last month, took a keen interest in the trials and tribulations of the Warriors. She was known for both her skill and competitiveness as a tennis player. Well into her 100th year, she remained an accomplished mahjong player who thoroughly enjoyed the company of the ladies with whom she played. Lillian and Bob were members of Temple Sinai continuously since 1956 and Claremont Country Club for over 25 years. In her younger years, she was an active member of her socially conscious sorority, Theta Delta Xi. articles.text: On Wednesday, March 8, eighteen Piedmont Seniors ventured to KQED’s new facility on Mariposa Street in San Francisco, where the group was able to see both the television and the radio studios. KQED’s new building now incorporates state of the art technology, as almost everything now is computerized and is managed in the control booths. Even the camera movements are done remotely. The Piedmont Seniors also were able to see the studio where Leslie Sbrocco hosts the popular show “Check Please Bay Area”. The building is ADA accessible, allowing people with limited mobility to enjoy the studios. The elevators take visitors to the fourth floor for a breathtaking view of San Francisco. Two knowledgeable volunteer docents met with the Piedmont Seniors to provide an intimate tour. While there, the Seniors met the KQED CEO and President Michael Isip, who said “an informed, inspired and involved citizenry is the foundation of a healthy democracy.” KQED wants to spark curiosity and build bridges across people’s curiosity as they encourage diversity, creativity and trust. KQED’s mission is public service by providing the community with an alternative to commercial media so the public can make more informed decisions regarding politics and other differing opinions. KQED first went on the air in 1954 and was predominantly used for quality children’s programs. It is a non-profit, non-commercial entity that relies on public donations in the form of grants, endowments and bequests. Federal funding through the Corporation for Public Broadcasting makes up less than 10% of its budget. KQED encourages students to explore the facility so they can be exposed to new people, places, and ideas. The station also includes regular free podcasts in addition to their radio and television broadcasts. After the tour, the Piedmont Seniors headed to the Embarcadero for a tasty luncheon at Atwater Tavern. This was the first time the group has been welcomed at the entrance to a restaurant by its owner. Parking is always difficult in San Francisco, but the owner had reserved some spots for the Seniors. The upstairs provides a lovely view of the waterfront and is often used for parties, special events and wedding receptions. The Seniors’ driver, Jim Ayotte, who happens to also be a member of the Piedmont Seniors, is very knowledgeable about the terrain of San Francisco. So, as an extra highlight of the day he acted as a tour guide, and was eager to point out the newer buildings, and give the group some history of the area. By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I am going to be traveling. My neighbor just came back from being overseas and her phone was hacked. What kind of precautions can I take to prevent that from happening to me? Bert C., Oakland Dear Bert: Your timing on that question is excellent because the FBI just put out a statement last week for travelers and the public to avoid using free charging stations in airports, hotels, restaurants and shopping centers. They said in their announcement that hackers have found a way to use public USB ports to introduce malware, and even monitoring software onto devices. Devices like iPhones, and iPads, with compromised USB cables can be hijacked through software that can access usernames and passwords. When we travel by air, it seems like a welcome convenience that we can just plug our phones and iPads into USB ports that are often in the waiting area of the gate. It’s nice not to have to carry the charger, and just carry the USB cable. And, of course, more and more airlines, have these ports available right at your seat, even in economy. But according to the FBI, and cyber security experts, this is not safe. So, what are you to do when you must travel for many hours and your devices run out of juice? Just carry your own charger and plug it into an available electrical outlet instead. Yes, it’s bulkier, but it’s nothing compared to the nightmare of having your device hacked and even in some cases your identity stolen. This warning by the FBI is not new, the FCC has warned about “juice jacking” (as the malware and hacking scheme is called) since 2021. More and more, bad actors are finding a way to get into our devices. So, as we load more sensitive information onto our devices, we have to be more vigilant. The same caution applies to using public Wi-Fi, whether it’s in a hotel or airport, or coffee shop. If you must use public Wi-Fi, make sure you do not log into any sites that require a password, because hackers could be using software to capture sensitive information, like credit card numbers, and of course usernames and passwords. So, for example, sitting in an airport on the public Wi-Fi is not a good time to log into your bank, or to log into a retail site and use your credit card to buy something. If you must do work or have access to a site where you need to put in sensitive information, it’s vital that you subscribe to a VPN, which is a Virtual Private Network. This type of service encrypts your activity on the web and keeps your identity hidden while surfing. Some of the top reviewed VPNs are CyberGhost, Private Internet Access, NordVPN, and there are several more. Also, make sure your device is not set to automatically connect to available Wi-Fi networks. If you don’t need it, turn Bluetooth off also. Change your passwords to sites you may visit online before you travel, and then change them again when you get home. When you are on the website, make sure it says “https” instead of just “http” (the “s” stands for “secure”). And, of course, when you get back home, check your credit card statements for any unrecognized charges. Enjoy your trip but be careful out there. articles.text: When we read about Grandparenting today, how likely is it that we are really referring to Grandmothering? How often does the professional advice and guidance actually support the experience of the grandfathers in the family? Chances are, not often. To be fair, in most families where grandparents play a significant caregiving role, the majority of the care is likely to be provided by grandmothers. But perhaps it’s time to think more broadly about gender stereotyping for grandfathers. Many grandfathers today played a much more active role in the raising of their children than their own fathers did. A grandfather today who raised children in the 80’s and 90’s is likely to have changed diapers and read bedtime stories, have been active in Dad’s clubs, school boards, Scouts, and coached their children in all kinds of sports. They probably attended school parent events, knew who the pediatrician was, and filled out forms for camps. Many of these activities would have been unknown to their own fathers. But even if a dad wasn’t a hands-on parent of little ones when he was young, the role of grandfather may be just what he has been waiting for his whole life. Some men may see this period in their life as a time to redeem themselves if they were less than present when his children were small. Maybe Grandpa regrets how much he was away on business, or how often he had to work nights and weekends, or maybe he just feels that the women in the family subtly nudged him out of a caregiving role he might have enjoyed. If the role of grandfather comes at a time when a man may have fewer professional pressures and obligations, if he is fit and healthy, and desires a meaningful role with his grandchildren, the possibilities for him are endless. The first step for a family is actually recognizing a grandfather’s hopes and dreams for his role. New parents may minimize the kinds of things they can expect from a new grandfather, and overemphasize a grandmother’s role. But whereas a grandmother may feel delighted to be able to use some of her skills and experience from years ago, a grandfather may be feeling a sense that he can now offer a young child something he didn’t manage to offer when he was a young father. Men are grandparents, too. They delight in their grandchildren, want to see them safe and healthy, and want to teach them many things that they feel are important for success in life. Some grandfathers may worry that the family doesn’t trust them with the care of small children, or maybe they are only thought of as financial supporters. But many have a deep desire to be close to grandchildren and to have a significant and meaningful role in their lives. If you are a grandfather, speak your truth to your family and let them know what you are hoping for as the years go on. If you want to be more involved with caregiving but feel unsure of yourself, find out how to get more education about childcare today. Seek support from other grandfathers if you can find it in your area or online. Make sure that your family knows what legacy you’d like to leave after you’re gone. If your children have a grandfather, open your mind to what he may have to offer your children. Ask him to share his feelings about being a grandfather. You might be very surprised by what you learn.
